the impact of employee sensitivity to the violent manifestations of ethnopolitical conflict on the organizational commitment of employees in firms operating in a violent operating context.
the impact of employee sensitivity to conflict on organizational commitment.
the role of organizational commitment in the management of foreign firms in an operating environment besets with ethnopolitical conflict.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results suggest that an operating context beset by violent ethnopolitical conflicts may extract an indirect cost on organizations through lowered employee commitment and that foreign-investment firms through a ‘‘foreignness advantage’’ can manage this potential loss by maintaining a high-level of perceived organizational support amongst its employees.

organizational commitment in a time of war is a complex phenomenon that is affected by a number of different factors and that the relationship between organizational commitment and employee sensitivity to war is mediated by a number of other variables, including perceived organizational support.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

employee sensitivity to violent ethnopolitical conflicts is negatively associated with organizational commitment, and that the negative relationship is attenuated when employees perceive high levels of organizational support.

employee sensitivity to the violent manifestations of ethnopolitical conflict has a negative impact on organizational commitment and this impact is attenuated for foreign-invested employees through a ‘foreign advantage’ in the form of perceived organizational support.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the management of foreign-invested enterprises (FIEs) operating in ethnopolitical conflict zones may be able to mitigate the potential negative impact of such conflict on their employees’ organizational commitment through the maintenance of high levels of perceived organizational support (POS).
employee sensitivity to violent ethnopolitical conflicts is an important predictor of organizational commitment, and that this sensitivity can be managed through perceived organizational support.

employee sensitivity to the operating environment may have important implications for organizational commitment, particularly in foreign-investment firms operating in violent ethnopolitical environments.
